lines.text: Do you know how hurricanes work? The biggest storms on Earth are giant heat engines, and their fuel is warm ocean water.
It starts over tropical seas warmer than about twenty six degrees Celsius. Warm, wet air rises off the surface.
As it rises, it cools, and the water vapour turns into towering clouds. That releases heat, which makes the air rise even faster.
Rising air leaves low pressure at the surface, so more air rushes in from all sides to fill the gap.
But Earth is turning, and that bends the incoming air. It's called the Coriolis effect. So the whole storm starts to spin: counterclockwise in the north, clockwise in the south.
In the middle, air sinks, forming a calm, clear eye. Around it, the eyewall holds the strongest winds, over two hundred and fifty kilometers per hour in the worst storms.
Once it moves over land or cold water, the fuel runs out, and the storm slowly falls apart.
So every hurricane is the ocean's heat, turned into wind.
